newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF team visits Bulgaria for currency board talks.
newsitem.headline: IMF team visits Bulgaria for currency board talks.

text.p: A delegation from the International Monetary Fund arrived in Sofia on Tuesday to complete preparations for a restrictive fixed exchange rate mechanism to stabilise the economy.
Mission leader Anne McGuirk said the latest wage rises announced last month might be rather high but welcomed the fact that April inflation had been below zero after sharp rises early in the year.
"We will be re-doing the macroeconomic framework and the budget taking into account the recent developments," she told reporters at Sofia airport on arrival.
The minimum wage was increased with effect from May 1 to 41,290 levs ($27.50) from 29,920 levs but most salaries are rather higher.
Under the currency board system, due to be introduced in mid-year, the amount of levs in circulation should be matched exactly by the amount of foreign exchange reserves.
Stoyanov is expected on Wednesday to ask Ivan Kostov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces, to form a government after his party's victory in general elections on April 19.

Muravei Radev, former deputy chairman of the economic committee in the previous parliament, is expected to be the new finance minister, while interim deputy prime minister Alexander Bozhkov is expected to retain the industry portfolio, overseeing the restructuring of the unwieldy state sector.
Parliament is due to appoint a new central bank governor and management to operate the bank in a currency board system.

McGuirk, who expects to stay about two weeks in Bulgaria, said the new central bank team could include a foreign adviser, but neither she nor central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov would identify any candidate.
A number of foreign economists have been advising President Petar Stoyanov and the interim government.

Asked whether the lev would be pegged to the dollar or the mark in the currency board, Filipov said this was yet to be decided. The dollar is trading at a relatively high level on international foreign exchange markets compared to the mark.
"The answer is very simple -- if we want things to be easier for us now we must peg it to the dollar, if we want things to be easier for us in the future it must be the mark," Filipov said.
Filipov said on Friday he was prepared to step down once parliament decided whom to appoint as his successor to run the bank under a currency board.
